## Paper {'paper_id': 'voting-leaderboards', 'title': 'EXPLORING AND MITIGATING ADVERSARIAL MANIP-ULATION OF VOTING-BASED LEADERBOARDS', 'abstract': '1Google 2UC Berkeley 3Carnegie Mellon University 4Stanford University 5ETH Zurich ∗Lead author †Alphabetical order', 'pdf_parse': {'paper_id': 'voting-leaderboards', 'abstract': [{'text': '1Google 2UC Berkeley 3Carnegie Mellon University 4Stanford University 5ETH Zurich ∗Lead author †Alphabetical order', 'section': 'Abstract', 'sec_num': None}], 'body_text': [{'text': 'Reliably evaluating the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs; e.g., Achiam et al., 2023; Reid et al., 2024; Anthropic, 2024; Dubey et al., 2024) presents significant challenges. Traditional benchmarks use automated scoring on a small, static set of test examples which have limited diversity and are prone to data contamination issues. Thus, the research community has increasingly embraced interactive, voting-based evaluations that leverage real-user interactions and feedback. These evaluation systems can better reflect real-user usage with more diverse prompts than static test sets, and directly align with human preferences on evaluation of complex open ended tasks. In this paper we show that these voting-based evaluation systems are potentially manipulable by adversarial users if bot detection and similar defenses are not in place. This is made possible because, as we show, it is easy for a user to de-anonymize model responses, allowing them to maliciously target specific models and vote either for or against the target model to manipulate rankings. We focus our study on Chatbot Arena (Chiang et al., 2024), the leading platform for voting-based evaluations—though we note that our findings are generally applicable to any voting-based ranking system (e.g., those in Lu et al. (2024); Li et al. (2024)). In Chatbot Arena, users perform headto-head model comparisons as follows: 1) a user submits a prompt, 2) two models are randomly selected and anonymously presented to the user, 3) the user votes for the better response, and 4) the voting results are incorporated into the leaderboard and the model identities are revealed (see Figure 1: Chatbot Arena compiles a model leaderboard using crowdsourced user votes and is therefore vulnerable to manipulation through adversarial voting. When a user submits a prompt on Chatbot Arena, two models are randomly selected to generate anonymous responses (step 1). Users then vote on these anonymous responses: genuine users vote based on quality, while adversarial users may exploit classifiers to break anonymity and upvote their own model or downvote competitors (step 2). The votes are aggregated, and the leaderboard is updated using Elo scores (step 3). As a result, adversarial voting can distort the model rankings. Fig. 1). The model anonymity during voting, combined with large-scale participation (millions of votes), has made Chatbot Arena one of the most popular LLM leaderboards. We introduce a reranking attack against voting-based and anonymous LLM ranking systems that allows an adversarial user to rank their target model higher or lower: 1. Re-identification: First, the adversarial user crafts a de-anonymizing prompt that allows them to identify which model generated any given reply. 2. Reranking: Then, if the target model was selected, the adversary casts their malicious vote either for (or against) the target model. Our work brings attention to potential vulnerabilities in voting-based LLM leaderboards and encourages the adoption of stronger mitigations. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We show that users can break model response anonymity on the Chatbot Arena platform with high efficacy ( > 9 5 \\% accuracy for a target model) on a diverse set of prompts (Section 2). • Through extensive simulations, we estimate that a few thousand adversarial votes are needed for an attacker to boost or reduce a model’s ranking (Section 3). • Finally, we develop a cost model for the attack and discuss the landscape of potential mitigations as well as their effectiveness (Section 4). Responsible disclosure. We disclosed this vulnerability with Chatbot Arena in August 2024, and have worked closely with them to analyze the risks and to identify and implement mitigations1. Note from Chatbot Arena. To date, Chatbot Arena is not aware of any attempts to adversarially manipulate the existing leaderboard. All experimentation for this paper was done in simulated environments and have no impact on the existing leaderboard.', 'section': 'INTRODUCTION', 'sec_num': '1'}, {'text': 'To obtain unbiased user feedback, it is crucial that the random pair of models chosen is presented anonymously to the user (see Figure 1), as anonymity makes it much harder for adversarial users to game the rankings. One simple strategy is to select a diverse set of prompts from various distributions, and then score each prompt on its ability to distinguish a set of models (see Section 2.4). Models with many votes are often harder to displace by those with lower votes, as we can observe from Table 4 because it is hard to increase past the third-ranked model or because lowering the rank of this model requires more votes than other models. Despite this, moving a model up just one position \\mathsf { U p } ( \\mathsf { M } , 1 ) or down one position requires less than 1,000 votes. Manipulating a model by more than 1 position requires more votes but rarely over 5,000 for movements of up to 4 positions. Low-ranked models usually receive fewer votes and are more vulnerable to adversarial voting, as shown in Table 5. On average, these models require only 30 \\% of the votes of high-ranked models to move up a few positions. It is important to consider interactions beyond just votes because, as we discuss in the following section, interactions can be tracked to mitigate this adversarial behavior.', 'section': 'RESULTS', 'sec_num': '3.2'}, {'text': 'We now discuss potential defenses against the adversarial manipulation of language model leaderboard’s like Chatbot Arena’s. Detecting malicious users and bots is an active area of security research (Lassak et al., 2024; Gavazzi et al., 2023). Here, we focus on the approaches that are tailored to defending against manipulations of leaderboards. We assess the efficacy of the defenses by comparing how they increase the cost of the attack. To facilitate this analysis, we first develop a cost model for our attack in (Section 4.1), followed by an analysis of each mitigation in Section 4.2.', 'section': 'MITIGATIONS', 'sec_num': '4'}, {'text': 'We formalize our cost measurement as follows. Let c represent the cost of the attack. Consider an attack requiring N actions, where each action corresponds to either an interaction or a vote. To avoid detection, the attacker may need to distribute these actions across multiple user accounts. Let m be the maximum number of actions permitted per user account, and c _ { \\mathrm { a c c o u n t } } the cost of obtaining a single user account. The total cost of the attack consists of three components: • Training detector cost c _ { \\mathsf { d e t e c t o r } } : the one-time cost of building the training-based, target-model detector offline. • Account maintenance \\mathrm { c o s t } = \\ \\lceil N / m \\rceil \\times c _ { \\mathrm { a c c o u n t } } : Multiple accounts become necessary when defensive mechanisms implement behavioral analytics to detect suspicious patterns, forcing attackers to distribute actions across accounts to evade detection. • Action cost N \\times c _ { \\mathrm { a c t i o n } } : the aggregate cost of all actions, where { \\mathcal { C } } _ { \\mathrm { a c t i o n } } represents the cost per individual action. Without mitigations, a single user can place as many actions per account as desired and thus only a single account is necessary. Further, the cost per action is minimal. Therefore, the total cost is dominated by the training detector cost c _ { \\mathsf { d e t e c t o r } } which we estimated in Appendix B.1 to be \\ 440$ in our current experimental setup. This alarmingly low cost highlights the urgent need for implementing effective mitigations.6', 'section': 'ESTIMATING THE COST OF ATTACK', 'sec_num': '4.1'}, {'text': 'Given that the one-time training detector cost, c _ { \\mathsf { d e t e c t o r } } , is relatively fixed, an effective mitigation should focus on increasing either the account maintenance cost \\lceil N / m \\rceil \\times c _ { \\mathrm { a c c o u n t } } (Section 4.2.1, Section 4.2.2, Section 4.2.3) or the online action cost N \\times c _ { \\mathrm { a c t i o n } } (Section 4.2.4). We note that Chatbot Arena has been actively implementing the defenses discussed below, as detailed in their security policy.7 # 4.2.1 AUTHENTICATION The most effective method to increase the cost per account c _ { \\mathrm { a c c o u n t } } is to enforce authentication on Chatbot Arena through integration with existing digital identity providers. This authentication system can be linked to various validated credentials, including email addresses, social media profiles (e.g., Twitter, Facebook), or phone numbers. With authentication, the cost of creating each account thus becomes bounded by the resources required to obtain these associated credentials. Riskbased authentication or multi-factor authentication may also be offered through some digital identity providers to increase c _ { \\mathrm { a c c o u n t } } with limited impact to benign users (Makowski & Pöhn, 2023; Gavazzi et al., 2023). Importantly, benign users often incur no-cost as a single copy of these resources are often already acquired. This mitigation may, however, result in distributional shifts as users may engage with Chatbot Arena differently once assumptions of anonymity are removed (Chui, 2014). # 4.2.2 RATE LIMITING Reducing m through temporal rate limits on actions for each account is also an effective strategy. Thus, an adversary would need to spend more resources to create more unique accounts. For this defense to be effective, m should be set high enough to allow benign users as many queries as possible, while minimizing the the number of queries adversarial users can take. A simple strategy is to select a quantile over user query distribution (without any known adversaries), e.g., the median. With estimates for the benign query distribution, the choice in m can be refined. # 4.2.3 MALICIOUS USER IDENTIFICATION Risk-based authentication (Gavazzi et al., 2023) in general leverages user behavior patterns to identify malicious users and increase their action costs. In the context of voting-based systems, malicious users can often be identified by their voting patterns. Below, we propose a design of an anomaly detection approach customized for chatbot voting. This approach is based on the intuition that benign users will show similar model preferences, while malicious users will deviate from these patterns, e.g., by voting for specific models more often. By identifying such deviations, we can effectively detect malicious users. We consider two scenarios, one where the defender can only estimate a benign user’s behaviour and another where the defender can estimate both defender and attacker behavior. # Scenario 1: Known Benign Distribution In this scenario, we assume that a defender can estimate the expected behaviour for benign users using historical data from previous votes. Now, if an adversary behaves significantly differently from the expected behaviour, the defender can detect it. To do so, we use a likelihood test to differentiate between the null hypothesis H _ { \\mathrm { b e n i g n } } that the user’s voting pattern matches the known benign distribution or the alternative hypothesis H . ¬benign that the user is from a different source. Let \\boldsymbol { x } = ( x _ { 1 } , . . . , x _ { n } ) represent a sequence of observed impressions by a user, where each x _ { i } is an impression for one of the available models. Under the null hypothesis H _ { \\mathrm { b e n i g n } } , we assume these votes come from the known benign user profile. Also we assume each vote is independent of each other. The likelihood of observing the entire sequence under the null hypothesis is then: L ( x | H _ { \\mathrm { b e n i g n } } ) = \\prod _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \\operatorname* { P r } ( x _ { i } | H _ { \\mathrm { b e n i g n } } ) . To assess how extreme this observation is under the null hypothesis, we use the test statistic: T ( x ) = - 2 \\ln ( L ( x | H _ { \\mathrm { b e n i g n } } ) ) . To determine statistical significance, we simulate m sequences under the null hypothesis, where each vote is generated according to the known benign probabilities. For each simulated sequence s ^ { j } , we calculate its test statistic \\bar { \\boldsymbol { T } } ( s ^ { j } ) . The empirical \\mathsf { p } -value is then computed as: p = { \\frac { 1 } { m } } \\sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { m } I \\{ T ( s ^ { j } ) \\geq T ( x ) \\} where I \\{ \\} is the indicator function. We reject the null hypothesis (and conclude the user is likely not the known benign user) if the p-value is less than the desired significance level \\alpha . In particular we use \\alpha = 0 . 0 1 in our evaluations. # Scenario 2: Known Benign and Malicious Distributions Because the leaderboard is public, the adversary can use the published ratings and counts to make themselves more difficult to detect by mimicking the average user behavior. To this end, the defender can instead release perturbed rankings and counts to each user so as to reduce an attacker’s knowledge of the true values. Our primary attack involves training a classifier that can identify which language model system produced a given generation. This task is related to the much older task of authorship attribution—identifying the authors of anonymous (but humanwritten) works of writing (Huang et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2020). Tay et al. Our framing of the task is easier than that of most prior work in this space because we assume the attacker has control over the prompt being used for generation, and the set of possible model configurations which may have been used for generation is fairly constrained. Detection via watermarking. There has been a slew of recent research aiming to watermark generated text to identify whether given text was generated with a particular, watermarked model (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023; Kuditipudi et al., 2024; Christ et al., 2024). We focus on this paper in validating one straightforward attack: by identifying and selectively voting for (or against) a particular model, an adversary can significantly alter the ordering of the best models. Mitigating this attack is feasible, and we are actively collaborating with the Chatbot Arena team to make Chatbot Arena more robust. We also encourage the community to explore and adopt mitigation strategies, such as voter authentication, rate limits, and more robust mechanisms for detecting malicious activities. Overview This plan outlines steps to reproduce the key experiments from the paper **“Exploring and Mitigating Adversarial Manipulation of Voting-Based Leaderboards”**. The work has three main experimental pillars: 1. **De‑anonymization of model responses** (Section 2) - Identity‑probing detector (simple keyword matching) - Training‑based detector (supervised classification on response features) - Using 8 prompt categories (English, Chinese, Spanish, Indonesian, Persian, Coding, Math, Safety‑violating) - Features: BoW, TF‑IDF, response length; classifier: logistic regression 2. **Adversarial vote simulation** (Section 3) - Simulate a leaderboard using Bradley‑Terry / Elo updates - Inject an attacker with a specified detector accuracy (default 95%, symmetric error) - Measure number of votes and interactions required to shift a model’s rank by *x* positions 3. **Mitigation evaluation** (Section 4, optional but valuable) - Likelihood‑based malicious‑user detection using simulated benign/attack voting patterns - Effect of releasing perturbed leaderboard rankings We will implement all parts from scratch, as no official code was released. Where precise data is unavailable (e.g., the internal 1.67‑million‑vote Chatbot Arena dataset), we will construct reasonable synthetic substitutes. --- ### 2. Resources & Data Requirements #### 2.1 Models to be used The paper evaluates **22 models** (Appendix A.1, Table 6). We will reproduce experiments using at least a representative subset, prioritising open‑source/accessible models to minimise API costs. **Recommended core subset** (can be expanded): `claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620`, `gemini-1.5-pro`, `gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18`, `llama-3.1-70b-instruct`, `mixtral-8x7b-instruct-v0.1`, `qwen2-72b-instruct`, `gemma-2-27b-it` Access methods: - **Proprietary** (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) – via their official APIs - **Open‑source** (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma) – via `Together AI` Inference API or local run (e.g., using `vLLM`/`transformers`). We will use Together to keep parity with the paper. **Cost note:** Data collection for training detectors requires roughly 200 prompts × 50 responses × 22 models; this can be expensive with paid APIs. For initial prototyping we may reduce the number of models and prompts, but the final reproduction should match the paper’s scale. A ballpark cost ~$440 is mentioned (Appendix A.3). #### 2.2 Prompt datasets The **training‑based detector** uses prompts from the following sources (Table 1): - **High‑resource normal chat:** English, Chinese, Spanish – sampled from `LMSYS-Chat-1M` - **Low‑resource normal chat:** Indonesian, Persian – sampled from `LMSYS-Chat-1M` - **Speciality prompts:** - *Coding* – `Alpaca Code` (or `HumanEval`) - *Math* – `MATH` dataset - *Safety‑violating* – `AdvBench` (Zou et al., 2023) We need to download or access these datasets. LMSYS‑Chat‑1M is available on Hugging Face. For coding we can use the “Alpaca Code” instruction dataset; for MATH, the original dataset. For AdvBench, we can use the provided harmful prompts (just for research purpose; we’ll treat them carefully). **Sampling strategy:** Randomly select **200 prompts per category** (total 1600 prompts). The paper uses 200 prompts per category in the main experiments. For testing, we can initially use fewer (e.g., 20 per category) and later scale up. #### 2.3 Historical voting data for simulation The paper’s simulations (Section 3) are based on an anonymised dataset of 1.67M votes from Chatbot Arena. This dataset is **not publicly available**. We will instead: - Build a **synthetic leaderboard** mimicking the Chatbot Arena statistics. - **Approach A (preferred):** Use the public Chatbot Arena Bradley‑Terry coefficients (available on their website with confidence intervals) to initialize model strengths. Simulate “genuine” user interactions using an Elo ranking system: sample pairs of models, compute win probability via the Bradley‑Terry formula, and record outcomes. - **Approach B:** Create a completely artificial rating pool (e.g., 130 models with normally distributed scores) and generate votes accordingly. We will adopt Approach A because it grounds the simulation in realistic relative strengths. The number of models can be set to ~130 as in the paper’s low‑end tables. **Vote generation details:** - For each “genuine” interaction, randomly pick two models uniformly (like in Arena). - Calculate win probability: *P(i beats j) = 1 / (1 + exp((rating_j – rating_i)/s))*, where `s` is a scaling factor (standard is 400 in Elo, but Chatbot Arena uses `s=1` in Bradley‑Terry? Actually they use logistic parameter equal to 1 in BT, so we set *s=1*). - Include ties: the arena allows “tie”, “both are bad”. We can fix a tie probability (e.g., the paper reports ~34.5% of votes are ties). We can sample tie with probability equal to historical fraction. - After each genuine vote, update the Elo rating of the two models using standard Elo update (K‑factor). We’ll tune K to keep dynamics plausible (small K like 4). Alternatively, we can simply collect thousands of outcomes without incremental rating updates based on the current ratings (but simulation of attack requires rating changes). **Attack simulation:** The attacker targets a specific model. When the target model is selected in a random pair, the attacker uses the detector (with given accuracy) to decide whether to cast a biased vote. The detector’s false‑positive/negative rates are symmetric 5% when accuracy=95%. If the detector says “target model”, the attacker votes *for* or *against* the target, otherwise abstains (or can adopt a non‑target strategy as ablations). The vote outcome (win/loss/tie) is set arbitrarily by the attacker: e.g., always “target wins” to boost ranking. We update Elo accordingly. #### 2.4 Computational environment - Python 3.10+ with standard data science libraries (`numpy`, `pandas`, `scikit-learn`, `matplotlib`, `scipy`). - API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Together AI. - Optional: `transformers` for tokenization or local inference if needed. - Storage: enough to save ~1600 prompts × 50 responses × 22 models ≈ 1.7M text strings (manageable on disk). --- ### 3. ## Logic Analysis for `responses.py`

### 1. Module Purpose
The `ResponseCollector` class is responsible for gathering the raw text responses from all language models on all prompts required for the **training‑based detector** (Section 2 of the paper). It orchestrates:

- Sampling prompts from each category using `PromptLoader`
- Querying each model via `ModelAPI` to obtain multiple responses per prompt (to capture generation variability)
- Persisting all collected data to disk (JSON cache per category) to avoid costly re‑queries during subsequent runs

This module is critical because the training‑based detector needs balanced datasets of 50 positive (target model) and 50 negative (other models) responses per prompt. The collector must ensure that for every (prompt, model) pair exactly `config.num_responses_per_prompt` (default 50) responses are stored.

### 2. Data Structures and State

- **`self.config`**: `Config` object – provides all parameters (model list, cache directory, number of prompts/responses, API retries, etc.)
- **`self.api`**: `ModelAPI` object – unified interface to query any model
- **`self.loader`**: `PromptLoader` object – supplies prompts from each category
- **`self.cache_dir`**: path string – directory where per‑category JSON files are saved. Created if missing.
- **`self.cache`**: `Dict[str, Any]` – in‑memory dictionary that mirrors the cached JSON files. Keys are prompt texts; values are dictionaries of the form `{model_name: [response_1, response_2, ..., response_N]}`.
- Optional: a `_temp_cache` to avoid reloading from disk repeatedly, but we can keep `self.cache` always loaded for the current category.

### 3. Initialization – `__init__(self, config: Config, api: ModelAPI, loader: PromptLoader)`

```
def __init__(self, config, api, loader):
    self.config = config
    self.api = api
    self.loader = loader
    self.cache_dir = config.cache_dir
    os.makedirs(self.cache_dir, exist_ok=True)
```

No caching data is loaded at init; each category is loaded lazily when `collect_all()` or a getter is called.

### 4. Core Method: `collect_for_prompt(prompt: str, models: List[str]) -> Dict[str, List[str]]`

**Purpose:** For a single fixed prompt, query each model `num_responses_per_prompt` times, collecting all responses. Return a dict suitable for insertion into the category‑level cache.

**Detailed Logic:**

- Initialize result dict: `responses = {}`
- For each `model` in `models`:
  - `model_responses = []`
  - For `i` in `range(config.num_responses_per_prompt)`:
    - Call `self.api.query(model, prompt, max_tokens=config.max_output_tokens, temperature=config.temperature, top_p=config.top_p)`
    - Append returned string to `model_responses`
    - (API wrapper already handles retries and possibly sleeps between calls; if not, add `time.sleep(config.api.request_interval)` to avoid rate limits.)
  - `responses[model] = model_responses`
- Return `responses`

**Potential issues:**
- If an API call permanently fails (e.g., model unavailable), we can log a warning and store an empty list or a special placeholder (like `None`). However, for fidelity, we expect all models to be reachable; the paper used the same APIs. We may implement a fallback: retry a few times, then raise an exception so the user can intervene.
- The method does **not** cache itself; it always calls the API. The caching layer is at the category level in `collect_all`.

### 5. Main Orchestration: `collect_all(self) -> None`

**Purpose:** Iterate over all categories defined in `config.prompt_categories`, sample prompts, collect missing responses, and persist each category to its own JSON file.

**Detailed Logic:**

- `for category, _ in config.prompt_categories.items():`
  - Load existing cache for this category if present, else empty dict.
  - `category_cache_path = os.path.join(self.cache_dir, f"{category}.json")`
  - `if os.path.exists(category_cache_path):`
    - `category_cache = utils.load_json(category_cache_path)`
  - `else:`
    - `category_cache = {}`
- Sample prompts: `prompts = self.loader.sample_prompts(category, config.num_prompts_per_category)`
- For each `prompt` in `prompts`:
  - If `prompt` already in `category_cache` and for every model the number of stored responses equals `config.num_responses_per_prompt`, **skip** collection (cache hit). Otherwise, we re‑collect for that prompt to ensure completeness; we could also handle partial collections, but for simplicity, if any missing, we call `collect_for_prompt` and overwrite or merge. We'll decide to overwrite if the cached list length differs.
  - (Optional) check if the prompt is incomplete: if cached data exists but some model missing, we can call `collect_for_prompt` but only for the missing model? That complicates. Easiest: if the prompt entry is incomplete or missing, call `collect_for_prompt(prompt, config.models)` and replace `category_cache[prompt]` with the fresh full dict. (Overwriting ensures consistency.)
  - Call `self.collect_for_prompt(prompt, config.models)` → `new_data`
  - `category_cache[prompt] = new_data`
  - Using `tqdm` to show progress: wrap the prompt loop with `tqdm(prompts, desc=f"Category {category}")`.
- After processing all prompts, save `category_cache` back to `category_cache_path` via `utils.save_json(category_cache_path, category_cache)`.
- Keep the in‑memory `self.cache` (we could set `self.cache = category_cache` for the last processed category, but better to manage per‑category: we can have a dictionary `self.all_cache[category] = category_cache`. That would allow retrieval later.

**Enhancement:** To support later access by the detector, we should maintain a per‑category cache in memory, e.g., `self.categories_cache = {}` (dict mapping category name to loaded cache). During `collect_all()`, we populate this structure and persist to disk. Then we can add a getter.

### 6. Caching Mechanism

- **Storage format:** Per‑category JSON files in `config.cache_dir`, named `{category}.json`.
- **JSON structure:**
  ```json
  {
    "prompt_text_1": {
      "model_a": ["resp1", "resp2", ...],
      "model_b": ["resp1", "resp2", ...]
    },
    "prompt_text_2": { ... }
  }
  ```
  This is readable but can become large; a future improvement could use compressed pickle, but JSON is fine for prototyping.
- **Integrity:** Every time a prompt is collected, we ensure exactly `num_responses_per_prompt` responses per model are stored.
- **Invalidation:** If any parameter changes (e.g., model list, `num_responses_per_prompt`, prompt sampling seed), the cache must be manually deleted or a version tag could be embedded. For simplicity, we do not auto‑invalidate; the user can delete the cache directory to force re‑collection.

### 7. Getter Methods (needed by `detector.py`)

The design only shows `collect_for_prompt` and `collect_all`, but `TrainingDetector` must access the collected responses. We must add a method to retrieve responses for a given category and prompt, or for a specific (prompt, model) pair.

Because the detector will iterate over categories and prompts, we can provide:

- `get_category_cache(category: str) -> Dict[str, Dict[str, List[str]]]`: loads and returns the full category cache from disk (or from `self.categories_cache` if already loaded). This is called by `TrainingDetector.evaluate_category`.
- Alternatively, `get_responses_for_prompt(prompt: str, model: str) -> List[str]`: but we would need to know the category. Not ideal.

We will implement `get_data(category: str) -> Dict`: if `self.categories_cache` has it, return; otherwise load from JSON and store in `self.categories_cache`. This ensures the detector doesn't re‑download.

**Adjustment to `collect_all`:** It should store the processed cache in `self.categories_cache[category]` after saving to disk, so that subsequent `get_data` calls are fast.

### 8. Error Handling & Rate Limiting

- **API retries:** `ModelAPI` already implements exponential backoff (as per shared knowledge). `ResponseCollector` does not need to add its own retries; it simply calls `self.api.query`.
- **Pacing:** Between successive API calls (for the same model) it is wise to sleep `config.api.request_interval` seconds to stay within rate limits. We can add `time.sleep(self.config.api.request_interval)` after each `query` inside the inner loop, but only for the same model? The API wrapper might enforce it globally. For safety, we'll add a small sleep after each query.
- **Missing models:** If a model consistently fails after retries, the exception propagates. In `collect_all`, we can wrap the `collect_for_prompt` call in a try‑except and log the error, then continue with other prompts, but this might leave incomplete data. Better to fail fast so the user can fix API keys. Therefore, we do not catch; let it propagate.
- **File I/O errors:** `save_json` may fail (e.g., disk full). We propagate; no silent failures.

### 9. Configuration Dependencies

The class heavily relies on:
- `config.models`: the list of model identifiers (strings matching API requirements)
- `config.prompt_categories`: mapping from category name to dataset identifier (used by `PromptLoader` to load the right dataset, not directly by this class)
- `config.num_prompts_per_category`: number of prompts to sample (e.g., 200)
- `config.num_responses_per_prompt`: responses per (prompt, model) pair (e.g., 50)
- `config.max_output_tokens`: generation `max_tokens` (512)
- `config.temperature` and `config.top_p`: if `null`, pass `None` to API (the API uses its own default)
- `config.cache_dir`: where to store JSON files
- `config.api.request_interval`: pacing

### 10. Integration in `main.py`

In `main.py`, the following sequence will occur:

```python
api = ModelAPI(config)
loader = PromptLoader(config)
collector = ResponseCollector(config, api, loader)
collector.collect_all()    # populates caches on disk and in memory
```

Later, when building the detector:
```python
detector = TrainingDetector(config, feature_extractor, collector)   # detector receives collector reference
detector.run_full_evaluation()   # internally calls collector.get_data(category) to get responses
```

Thus, `TrainingDetector` must accept a `ResponseCollector` instance (or we can pass just the cache data, but passing the collector keeps it simple). The design didn't show this parameter, but it's reasonable to add.

### 11. Edge Cases & Considerations

- **Duplicate prompts:** If `PromptLoader` accidentally returns the same prompt twice (unlikely with random sampling, but possible if dataset is small), the cache will overwrite; that’s fine.
- **Large JSON files:** A category with 200 prompts * 7 models * 50 responses = 70,000 strings. JSON may be several MB. Acceptable for now.
- **Unicode and special characters:** JSON supports UTF‑8; we should ensure `json.dump` with `ensure_ascii=False`.
- **Resuming partial collection:** The implemented check in `collect_all` (if prompt not in cache or incomplete) allows incremental runs. If collection was interrupted, re‑running will fill missing prompts without re‑querying existing complete ones.
- **Memory usage:** Holding the entire cache for one category in memory (during collection) is fine; we don't need all categories in memory simultaneously. We can discard category cache after saving, except the last one maybe. But the getter can load on demand. Implement `self.categories_cache` as a dictionary that keeps only the currently needed category; using `functools.lru_cache` on `get_data` is an elegant alternative.

### 12. Pseudo‑code Outline

```python
class ResponseCollector:
    def __init__(self, config, api, loader):
        self.config = config
        self.api = api
        self.loader = loader
        self.cache_dir = config.cache_dir
        os.makedirs(self.cache_dir, exist_ok=True)
        self.categories_cache = {}  # cache in memory: category_name -> {prompt: {model: [responses]}}

    def collect_for_prompt(self, prompt, models):
        result = {}
        for model in models:
            model_resps = []
            for _ in range(self.config.num_responses_per_prompt):
                resp = self.api.query(
                    model, prompt,
                    max_tokens=self.config.max_output_tokens,
                    temperature=self.config.temperature,
                    top_p=self.config.top_p
                )
                model_resps.append(resp)
                time.sleep(self.config.api.request_interval)
            result[model] = model_resps
        return result

    def collect_all(self):
        for category in self.config.prompt_categories:
            cache_path = os.path.join(self.cache_dir, f"{category}.json")
            if os.path.exists(cache_path):
                cat_cache = load_json(cache_path)
            else:
                cat_cache = {}
            prompts = self.loader.sample_prompts(category, self.config.num_prompts_per_category)
            for prompt in tqdm(prompts, desc=f"Collecting {category}"):
                # check completeness
                if prompt in cat_cache and all(len(cat_cache[prompt].get(m, [])) == self.config.num_responses_per_prompt for m in self.config.models):
                    continue
                fresh_data = self.collect_for_prompt(prompt, self.config.models)
                cat_cache[prompt] = fresh_data
            save_json(cache_path, cat_cache)
            self.categories_cache[category] = cat_cache

    def get_data(self, category):
        if category not in self.categories_cache:
            cache_path = os.path.join(self.cache_dir, f"{category}.json")
            self.categories_cache[category] = load_json(cache_path) if os.path.exists(cache_path) else {}
        return self.categories_cache[category]
```

This logic fulfills the requirements and integrates smoothly with the rest of the pipeline.
